summary:
As climate change and human activity intensify global wildfires and agricultural burning, land managers and emergency responders rely on satellite data to anticipate risks and coordinate action. However, while satellites have monitored thermal hotspots for over two decades, our historical record is fragmented. Older MODIS sensors are nearing retirement and are being replaced by modern, higher-resolution VIIRS sensors. Because these instruments differ in spatial sensitivity and observation schedules, their raw datasets cannot be directly compared—leaving responders without a unified view of long-term fire patterns.

To bridge this gap, the challenge asks you to build an interactive web application through a two-phase approach:

Data Harmonization: Reconcile over twenty years of NASA FIRMS MODIS data with modern VIIRS observations, creating a seamless historical baseline where the originating sensor no longer skews the data.

Interactive Analytics: Develop an intuitive web platform where users can define a region of interest—by drawing on a map or entering coordinates—and explore specific timeframes.

details:
The project is an interactive web application that generates a unified "burning activity calendar" spanning over two decades. First, it harmonizes historical active fire hotspot records from retiring MODIS sensors with modern, higher-resolution VIIRS satellite data—normalizing differences in spatial sensitivity and observation schedules so the records can be compared directly. Users then select a custom region of interest (by drawing on an interactive map or entering coordinates) and a date range. The app processes the harmonized data to display visual timelines, seasonal heatmaps, and anomaly comparisons against multi-year historical medians, alongside downloadable CSV reports.

What benefits does it have? It eliminates data fragmentation between legacy and modern Earth Observation satellites, saving analysts from complex manual calibration. By translating raw thermal detections into intuitive, color-coded calendars and anomaly metrics, it allows users to instantly identify peak burning seasons, detect unusual fire spikes, and export clean, ready-to-use datasets.

What is the intended impact of the project? Designed for emergency responders, firefighters, land managers, and climate scientists, the tool strengthens early warning systems and resource allocation. By providing clear historical context for current fire activity, it supports proactive wildfire mitigation, smarter agricultural burn management, and improved protection of ecosystems, property, and human lives.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software are used?

  • Data Sources: NASA Earthdata FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot archives).
  • Data Processing & Backend: Python (using geospatial and data libraries like Pandas, GeoPandas, and NumPy) to harmonize sensor discrepancies and run statistical baseline comparisons.
  • Frontend & Mapping: JavaScript/TypeScript (React or Vue) paired with interactive mapping libraries (Leaflet or Mapbox GL) and data visualization tools (D3.js or Chart.js) to render the burning calendar and downloadable CSVs.
  • Hardware: Standard cloud servers for spatial database hosting and standard developer workstations.

How is the project creative? Instead of presenting raw satellite telemetry on a cluttered map, the project reframes over 20 years of multi-sensor thermal data into an intuitive "calendar" format. Combining sensor-agnostic statistical harmonization with accessible visual color ramps turns complex remote-sensing physics into an immediately readable diagnostic tool.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Sensor Discrepancies: Accounting for differences in spatial resolution (MODIS 1 km vs. VIIRS 375 m), detection sensitivity, and satellite overpass schedules so newer data doesn't artificially appear as an increase in fire activity.
  • Accessibility & Usability: Implementing colorblind-friendly color ramps and intuitive map-drawing tools so high-stress emergency managers can extract insights rapidly without needing remote-sensing expertise.
